claim: ILC1-like cells (ILC1lc) are significantly increased around lesional and non-lesional hair follicles of alopecia areata (AA) patients.
source: Here, we have explored the involvement of innate lymphoid cells-type 1 (ILC1) in the pathogenesis of alopecia areata (AA), because we found them to be significantly increased around lesional and non-lesional HFs of AA patients.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunofluorescence data and quantitative immunohistomorphometry showing increased ILC1lc in AA patient samples (Figure 1).

claim: ILC1lc induced premature, apoptosis-driven hair follicle regression (catagen) when co-cultured with healthy, stressed, organ-cultured human scalp hair follicles.
source: ILClc induced all hallmarks of AA ex vivo: they significantly promoted premature, apoptosis-driven HF regression (catagen), HF cytotoxicity/dystrophy, and most important for AA pathogenesis, the collapse of the HFs physiological immune privilege.
evidence: The manuscript presents data from ex vivo co-culture experiments showing catagen induction (Figure 6A).

claim: ILC1lc induced hair follicle cytotoxicity and dystrophy in ex vivo co-culture experiments.
source: ILClc induced all hallmarks of AA ex vivo: they significantly promoted premature, apoptosis-driven HF regression (catagen), HF cytotoxicity/dystrophy, and most important for AA pathogenesis, the collapse of the HFs physiological immune privilege.
evidence: The manuscript presents LDH release data (Figure 3) and morphological evidence of HF dystrophy (Figure 4).

claim: ILC1lc induced the collapse of the hair follicle's physiological immune privilege in ex vivo co-culture experiments.
source: ILClc induced all hallmarks of AA ex vivo: they significantly promoted premature, apoptosis-driven HF regression (catagen), HF cytotoxicity/dystrophy, and most important for AA pathogenesis, the collapse of the HFs physiological immune privilege.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunohistochemistry data showing altered expression of immune privilege markers (Figure 5).

claim: NKG2D-blocking antibodies antagonized the AA-inducing effects of ILC1lc in ex vivo experiments.
source: NKG2D-blocking or IFNγ-neutralizing antibodies antagonized this.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing reduced catagen induction and preserved immune privilege with NKG2D blocking antibodies (Figures 5 and 6A).

claim: IFNγ-neutralizing antibodies antagonized the AA-inducing effects of ILC1lc in ex vivo experiments.
source: NKG2D-blocking or IFNγ-neutralizing antibodies antagonized this.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing reduced catagen induction with IFNγ-neutralizing antibodies (Figure 6A).

claim: Intradermal injection of autologous activated, NKG2D+/IFNγ-secreting ILC1lc into healthy human scalp skin xenotransplanted onto SCID/beige mice induced characteristic AA lesions.
source: In vivo, intradermal injection of autologous activated, NKG2D+/IFNγ-secreting ILC1lc into healthy human scalp skin xenotransplanted onto SCID/beige mice sufficed to rapidly induce characteristic AA lesions.
evidence: The manuscript presents in vivo data showing hair loss and AA-like immunopathology in xenotransplants injected with ILC1lc (Figure 7).

claim: ILC1lc are positive for the ILC1 phenotype and negative for classical NK markers.
source: This provides the first evidence that ILC1lc, which are positive for the ILC1 phenotype and negative for the classical NK markers, suffice to induce AA in previously healthy human HFs ex vivo and in vivo
evidence: The manuscript presents FACS analysis data characterizing ILC1lc phenotype (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: AA is not always an autoantigen-dependent, CD8+T cell-driven autoimmune disease.
source: This provides the first evidence that ILC1lc, which are positive for the ILC1 phenotype and negative for the classical NK markers, suffice to induce AA in previously healthy human HFs ex vivo and in vivo, and further questions the conventional wisdom that AA is always an autoantigen-dependent, CD8 +T cell-driven autoimmune disease.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing ILC1lc alone can induce AA without CD8+ T cells, supported by anti-CD3 antibody experiments (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: AA is the most common inflammatory hair loss disorder.
source: Alopecia areata (AA) is both the most common inflammatory hair loss disorder and one of the most common human autoimmune diseases and exerts a major negative impact on quality of life (Gilhar et al., 2012; Gilhar et al., 2019a; Korta et al., 2018; Pratt et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: AA is one of the most common human autoimmune diseases.
source: Alopecia areata (AA) is both the most common inflammatory hair loss disorder and one of the most common human autoimmune diseases and exerts a major negative impact on quality of life (Gilhar et al., 2012; Gilhar et al., 2019a; Korta et al., 2018; Pratt et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: AA exerts a major negative impact on quality of life.
source: Alopecia areata (AA) is both the most common inflammatory hair loss disorder and one of the most common human autoimmune diseases and exerts a major negative impact on quality of life (Gilhar et al., 2012; Gilhar et al., 2019a; Korta et al., 2018; Pratt et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A causal therapy for AA does not yet exist.
source: Despite major recent advances in AA therapy, a causal therapy does not yet exist, and disease relapse after therapy discontinuation is the rule, not the exception in long-standing AA (Meah et al., 2020; Gilhar et al., 2019a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Disease relapse after therapy discontinuation is the rule in long-standing AA.
source: Despite major recent advances in AA therapy, a causal therapy does not yet exist, and disease relapse after therapy discontinuation is the rule, not the exception in long-standing AA (Meah et al., 2020; Gilhar et al., 2019a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The currently available AA therapy, including JAK inhibitors, is purely symptomatic and remains unsatisfactory.
source: Thus, the currently available, purely symptomatic AA therapy, including JAK inhibitors (Gilhar et al., 2019b), remains unsatisfactory.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The exact pathobiology of AA and its clinical variants remains to be fully characterized.
source: Since the exact pathobiology of AA and its clinical variants remains to be fully characterized, the – likely diverse – disease-initiating factors that ultimately result in the characteristic AA hair loss pattern shared by all AA variants, require more comprehensive dissection for optimal, personalized therapeutic targeting (Bertolini et al., 2020; Paus et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A classical, autoantigen- and CD8+T cell-dependent autoimmune variant of AA (AAA) and a possibly autoantigen-independent non-autoimmune variant (NAIAA) may have to be distinguished from each other.
source: Specifically, there is increasing awareness that a classical, autoantigen- and CD8 +T cell-dependent autoimmune variant of AA (AAA) and a possibly autoantigen-independent non-autoimmune variant (NAIAA) may have to be distinguished from each other (Gilhar et al., 2019a; Bertolini et al., 2020; Paus et al., 2018; Paus, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: AA shows a wide spectrum of phenotypes and sub-forms.
source: This is in line with the long-standing, but often under-appreciated clinical recognition that AA shows a wide spectrum of phenotypes and sub-forms (Gilhar et al., 2012; Ikeda, 1965; Meah et al., 2021; King et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Insufficient therapeutic targeting of innate immunocytes may be one reason why the currently available AA therapy is not entirely satisfactory.
source: One reason why the currently available AA therapy is not entirely satisfactory may be related to as yet insufficient therapeutic targeting of innate immunocytes in the immunopathogenesis of human AA, namely in NAIAA, even though these are now recognized as major players in AA pathobiology (Ghraieb et al., 2018; Ito et al., 2008; Li et al., 2016; Uchida et al., 2020; Uchida et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature and is an inference from the data presented.

claim: AA lesions are associated with a massive increase in the number of perifollicular NKG2D+NK cells.
source: Previously, we had demonstrated that AA lesions are associated with a massive increase in the number of perifollicular NKG2D+NK cells (Gilhar et al., 2013a), which recognize the activating NKG2D ligand MICA, a 'danger' signal that is greatly overexpressed by the epithelium of lesional AA HFs (Ito et al., 2008; Li et al., 2016; Connell and Jabbari, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: NKG2D+NK cells recognize the activating NKG2D ligand MICA.
source: Previously, we had demonstrated that AA lesions are associated with a massive increase in the number of perifollicular NKG2D+NK cells (Gilhar et al., 2013a), which recognize the activating NKG2D ligand MICA, a 'danger' signal that is greatly overexpressed by the epithelium of lesional AA HFs (Ito et al., 2008; Li et al., 2016; Connell and Jabbari, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MICA is a 'danger' signal that is greatly overexpressed by the epithelium of lesional AA hair follicles.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: NKG2D and its activating ligands play a key role in human and murine AA.
source: Subsequent work has confirmed the key role of NKG2D and its activating ligands in human and murine AA (Xing et al., 2014; Petukhova et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: AA lesions can be induced experimentally in healthy human scalp skin in vivo by the transfer of interleukin 2 (IL-2)-activated NKG2D+ cells.
source: In fact, AA lesions can be induced experimentally in healthy human scalp skin in vivo by the transfer of interleukin 2 (IL-2)-activated NKG2D+ cells (Gilhar et al., 2013a), most of which had NK cell characteristics, with only a small minority of CD8 +T cells being present, that is the best-recognized pathogenic lymphocyte population in AA (Gilhar et al., 2012; Gilhar et al., 2013a; Pratt et al., 2017; Bertolini et al., 2020; de Jong et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: CD8+T cells are the best-recognized pathogenic lymphocyte population in AA.
source: In fact, AA lesions can be induced experimentally in healthy human scalp skin in vivo by the transfer of interleukin 2 (IL-2)-activated NKG2D+ cells (Gilhar et al., 2013a), most of which had NK cell characteristics, with only a small minority of CD8 +T cells being present, that is the best-recognized pathogenic lymphocyte population in AA (Gilhar et al., 2012; Gilhar et al., 2013a; Pratt et al., 2017; Bertolini et al., 2020; de Jong et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Pro-inflammatory mast cells are increased around/in lesional human AA hair follicles.
source: Moreover, pro-inflammatory mast cells (Bertolini et al., 2014) and (likely autoantigen-non-specific) γδ T-cells are also increased around/in lesional human AA HFs (Uchida et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: γδ T-cells are increased around/in lesional human AA hair follicles.
source: Moreover, pro-inflammatory mast cells (Bertolini et al., 2014) and (likely autoantigen-non-specific) γδ T-cells are also increased around/in lesional human AA HFs (Uchida et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: γδ T-cells and mast cells suffice to induce the hallmarks of AA ex vivo.
source: Finally, these 'intermediate immunity' protagonists suffice to induce the hallmarks of AA ex vivo (Uchida et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Human ILC1 cells secrete large amounts of interferon-γ (IFN-γ).
source: We were interested in these immunocytes since human ILC1 cells secrete large amounts of interferon-γ (IFN-γ) (Ebbo et al., 2017), the crucial AA pathogenesis-promoting cytokine (Gilhar et al., 2012; Gilhar et al., 2019a; Paus et al., 2018), and this notably independent of classical autoantigen-specific CD8 +T cell activities.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: IFN-γ is the crucial AA pathogenesis-promoting cytokine.
source: We were interested in these immunocytes since human ILC1 cells secrete large amounts of interferon-γ (IFN-γ) (Ebbo et al., 2017), the crucial AA pathogenesis-promoting cytokine (Gilhar et al., 2012; Gilhar et al., 2019a; Paus et al., 2018), and this notably independent of classical autoantigen-specific CD8 +T cell activities.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: ILC1 cells secrete IFN-γ independent of classical autoantigen-specific CD8+T cell activities.
source: We were interested in these immunocytes since human ILC1 cells secrete large amounts of interferon-γ (IFN-γ) (Ebbo et al., 2017), the crucial AA pathogenesis-promoting cytokine (Gilhar et al., 2012; Gilhar et al., 2019a; Paus et al., 2018), and this notably independent of classical autoantigen-specific CD8 +T cell activities.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature and represents established knowledge about ILC1 biology.

claim: ILC1s are placed in strategic tissue locations.
source: These 'unconventional' T-cells are placed in strategic tissue locations (Collins et al., 2017; Jiao et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2021) and represent an important link between innate and adaptive immunity (Vivier et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: ILC1s represent an important link between innate and adaptive immunity.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: ILC1s play an essential role in human inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).
source: While ILC1s play an essential role in human inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) (Ebbo et al., 2017; Luo et al., 2022; Clottu et al., 2021), their role in the pathophysiology of autoimmune hepatitis and rheumatoid arthritis requires further investigation (Ebbo et al., 2017; Fang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2015), and their role in human autoimmune diseases overall remains insufficiently understood.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: ILC1 cells are classified as a component of type 1 immunity.
source: ILC1 cells are classified as a component of type 1 immunity (Shannon et al., 2021), express NKG2D, recognize conserved phosphoantigens (Nabekura and Shibuya, 2021a), and contribute to immunity against tumor cells, for example through NKG2D activation (Dadi et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The activating receptor NKG2D and its ligands (MICA, ULBP3) play an important role in innate (NK, ILC1), 'translational' (γδ T-cells) and CD8 T-cell-mediated immune responses to tumors and in several autoimmune diseases.
source: The activating receptor NKG2D and its ligands (MICA, ULBP3) play an important role in innate (NK, ILC1), 'translational' (γδ T-cells) and CD8 T-cell-mediated immune responses to tumors and in several autoimmune diseases (Frazao et al., 2019; Babic and Romagnani, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: ILC1 cells produce TH1-type cytokines such as IFN-γ.
source: Given that ILC1 cells produce TH1-type cytokines (such as IFN-γ) and share several phenotypic markers with NK cells, namely NKG2D (Spits et al., 2016), it is challenging to distinguish NKs and ILC1 cells (Tulic et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2018; Seillet et al., 2021; Conlon et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: ILC1 cells share several phenotypic markers with NK cells, namely NKG2D.
source: Given that ILC1 cells produce TH1-type cytokines (such as IFN-γ) and share several phenotypic markers with NK cells, namely NKG2D (Spits et al., 2016), it is challenging to distinguish NKs and ILC1 cells (Tulic et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2018; Seillet et al., 2021; Conlon et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: How to reliably discriminate between NK cells and ILC1s and unraveling the shared and distinct functions of these cell populations remains an important open quest.
source: In fact, how to reliably discriminate between NK cells and ILC1s and unraveling the shared and distinct functions of these cell populations remains an important open quest (Seillet et al., 2021; Lopes et al., 2023; Cheng et al., 2023; Taggenbrock and van Gisbergen, 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

source: For example, Eomeshi T-betlo liver-resident NK cells have been described in humans and mice (Park et al., 2019; Harmon et al., 2016), while ILC1s from human tonsil and blood was also found to be Eomes+ (Cella et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

source: For example, Eomeshi T-betlo liver-resident NK cells have been described in humans and mice (Park et al., 2019; Harmon et al., 2016), while ILC1s from human tonsil and blood was also found to be Eomes+ (Cella et al., 2019).

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: CD49a and integrin α2 (CD49b) are used as two mutually exclusive markers for distinguishing between NK and ILC1 cells, with NK cells being defined as CD49b+CD49a- and ILC1 as CD49b-CD49a+.
source: However, although integrin α1 (CD49a) is upregulated on activated NK cells (Albini et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2016), CD49a and integrin α2 (CD49b) are used as two mutually exclusive markers for distinguishing between NK and ILC1 cells, with NK cells being defined as CD49b+CD49a- and ILC1 as CD49b-CD49a+ (Gao et al., 2017; Vienne et al., 2021; Flommersfeld et al., 2021; Krzywinska et al., 2022)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

source: Also, in contrast to ILC1 and ILC1lc, classical NK cells demonstrate high T-bet and Eomes expression (T-bethi /Eomeshi) (Verma et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: ILC1lc are defined as CD49a+CD49b-.
source: Therefore, for the purpose of this study, we define ILC1lc as CD49a+CD49b- (Verma et al., 2020) and as lin-/CD127+/CD117-/CRTH2-phenotype, which are typical to classical ILC1 cells (Bennstein et al., 2020; Krabbendam et al., 2021), and also as T-betlo/ Eomeshi (Bennstein et al., 2020) (in contrast to classical T-bethi /Eomeslo ILC1 cells Verma et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature and represents the operational definition used in the study.

claim: ILC1lc are defined as lin-/CD127+/CD117-/CRTH2-phenotype.
source: Therefore, for the purpose of this study, we define ILC1lc as CD49a+CD49b- (Verma et al., 2020) and as lin-/CD127+/CD117-/CRTH2-phenotype, which are typical to classical ILC1 cells (Bennstein et al., 2020; Krabbendam et al., 2021), and also as T-betlo/ Eomeshi (Bennstein et al., 2020) (in contrast to classical T-bethi /Eomeslo ILC1 cells Verma et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature and represents the operational definition used in the study.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature and represents the operational definition used in the study.

claim: Only extremely few ILC1lc are present in healthy control skin.
source: This revealed the presence of only extremely few ILC1lc in healthy control skin with all three staining settings employed (Eomes+, CD49a+, NKG2D+ [Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A], Eomes+, c-KIT-, CD49a+ [Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A], or NKp44+, CD103+, T-bet- cells [Figure 1C and D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Kim, 2015; Fuchs et al., 2013; Salimi and Ogg, 2014]).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 1.

claim: ILC1lc in healthy scalp skin are preferentially scattered along the papillary dermis and around the hair follicles.
source: These cells appeared to be preferentially scattered along the papillary dermis of healthy scalp skin biopsies and around the HFs (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Intra and peri-follicular infiltrates of ILC1lc are frequently present in lesional AA hair follicles.
source: Instead, intra and peri-follicular infiltrates of ILC1lc were frequently present in lesional AA HFs (Figure 1A, B, C and D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), typically in conjunction with a dominant infiltrate of CD8+/NKG2D+ cells around the hair bulb (p<0.05) (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantitative immunohistomorphometry presented in Figure 1.

claim: The number of ILC1lc is significantly increased in/around non-lesional AA hair follicles compared to healthy scalp skin.
source: Importantly, the number of ILC1lc was already significantly increased in/around non-lesional AA HFs compared to healthy scalp skin (p<0.01) (Figure 1A, B, C and D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunohistomorphometry data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: ILC1lc may have arrived around the hair follicles before the CD8 cells and may have contributed to attracting the CD8 cells into the perifollicular space.
source: This may indicate that ILC1lc may actually have arrived around the HFs before the CD8 cells and may have contributed to attracting the CD8 cells into the perifollicular space.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that ILC1lc are increased in non-lesional AA skin.

claim: ILC1lc can be expanded from human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) in vitro using IL-2, IL-18, IL-33, and IL-12.
source: To facilitate ILC1lc isolation, PBMCs of healthy volunteers were first cultured with high-dose IL-2 (100 U/mL) in the presence of IL-18 (1 µg/1 ml), IL-33 (1.5 µg/5 ml), and IL-12 (1.5 µg/5 ml), since these cytokines induce ILC1lc expansion (Salimi and Ogg, 2014; Silver et al., 2016; Orimo et al., 2020; Ohne et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature and the experimental methods described.

claim: ILC1lc sorted by FACS Aria on day seven of culture showed low T-bet and high Eomes expression.
source: When ILC1lc were sorted by FACS Aria and characterized by FACS analysis on day seven of culture, low T-bet, and high Eomes expression were observed (Figure 2A), in contrast to classical T-bethi and Eomeslo ILC1 cells (Jiao et al., 2016; Vivier et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: ILC1lc expressed CD127+, CD161+, c-KIT-, and CRTH2-.
source: In addition, the ILC1lc expressed and shared the following markers with classical ILC1 cells: LIN- CD3/CD1a/D14/CD19/CD34/CD123/CD11c /BDCH2/FcεR1α/TCRαβ/TCRγδ/CD56, CD127+, CD161+, c-KIT-, and CRTH2- (Zook and Kee, 2016; Bernink et al., 2017; Simoni and Newell, 2017; Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: ILC1lc expressed high levels of integrin α1 (CD49a) combined with the absence of integrin α2 (CD49b).
source: Indeed, the FACS analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B and C) revealed that ILC1lc demonstrates the ILC1 phenotype (CD200R, CD127, CXCR6) (Lopes et al., 2023; Curio and Belz, 2022) but not of the classical NK cell lineage (IRF8, Perforin, NKp80, CD16) (Sagebiel et al., 2019; Brownlie et al., 2021; Krämer et al., 2023), thus further serving as an evidence that EOMES +ILCs represent distinct ILC1 lineage-defining markers. In contrast to NK cells, ILC1lc also expressed the expected high levels of integrin α1 (CD49a), combined with the absence of integrin α2 (CD49b) (Jiao et al., 2016; Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: ILC1lc are negative for IRF8, Perforin, NKp80, and CD16.
source: Indeed, the FACS analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B and C) revealed that ILC1lc demonstrates the ILC1 phenotype (CD200R, CD127, CXCR6) (Lopes et al., 2023; Curio and Belz, 2022) but not of the classical NK cell lineage (IRF8, Perforin, NKp80, CD16) (Sagebiel et al., 2019; Brownlie et al., 2021; Krämer et al., 2023)
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: ILC1lc are positive for CD200R, CD127, and CXCR6.
source: Indeed, the FACS analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B and C) revealed that ILC1lc demonstrates the ILC1 phenotype (CD200R, CD127, CXCR6) (Lopes et al., 2023; Curio and Belz, 2022) but not of the classical NK cell lineage (IRF8, Perforin, NKp80, CD16) (Sagebiel et al., 2019; Brownlie et al., 2021; Krämer et al., 2023)
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: ILC1lc are RORγt negative.
source: In order to exclude the possibility that contamination from ILC3s during sorting the ILC1lc and thus contributing to the observed results, we generated a new set of FACS data on sorted ILC1lc. Given that ILC1 cells are RORγt negative while ILC3 cells are RORγt positive (Peng et al., 2022; Fiancette et al., 2021), the data clearly demonstrate that the contamination hypothesis is highly unlikely (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: ILC1lc induced significantly higher LDH release from hair follicles than ILC2s, ILC3s, or PBMCs/PHA after three days of co-culture.
source: First, we studied the cytotoxic effects of ILC1lc on healthy human scalp HF ex vivo by measuring the HF release of LDH into the culture medium. This not only showed significantly higher LDH release induced by ILC1lc than by co-culture with all three negative control cell populations (ILC2s, ILC3s, or PBMCs/PHA) but also even higher HF cytotoxicity levels than those induced by CD8+/NKG2D+ cells (p<0.01), namely after three days of co-culture (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by LDH release assay data presented in Figure 3.

claim: ILC1lc induced even higher hair follicle cytotoxicity levels than CD8+/NKG2D+ cells after three days of co-culture.
source: First, we studied the cytotoxic effects of ILC1lc on healthy human scalp HF ex vivo by measuring the HF release of LDH into the culture medium. This not only showed significantly higher LDH release induced by ILC1lc than by co-culture with all three negative control cell populations (ILC2s, ILC3s, or PBMCs/PHA) but also even higher HF cytotoxicity levels than those induced by CD8+/NKG2D+ cells (p<0.01), namely after three days of co-culture (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by LDH release assay data presented in Figure 3.

claim: ILC1lc induced characteristic morphological signs of hair follicle dystrophy.
source: These HF cytotoxicity results were fully corroborated by characteristic morphological signs of HF dystrophy following co-culture with ILC1lc; while CD8+/NKG2D+ cells induced similar dystrophy phenomena, these were not seen after co-culture with PBMC/PHA (Figure 4A, B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by H&E staining data presented in Figure 4A-C.

claim: ILC1lc induced pathological melanin clumping and ectopically located intrafollicular melanin granules.
source: The induction of significant HF dystrophy by ILC1lc ex vivo was further documented by the presence of pathological melanin clumping and ectopically located intrafollicular melanin granules (Bodó et al., 2007; Hendrix et al., 2005; Figure 4D, E, F and G)
evidence: The claim is supported by Masson-Fontana histochemistry data presented in Figure 4D-G.

claim: ILC1lc induced decreased proliferation and increased apoptosis of hair matrix keratinocytes.
source: and by decreased proliferation and increased apoptosis of hair matrix keratinocytes (Figure 4H, I, J and K). Both were also seen in the CD8+/NKG2D+group (positive control), but not in HFs co-cultured with PBMCs/PHA (negative control) (p<0.001, p<0.01, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by Ki-67/TUNEL staining data presented in Figure 4H-K.

claim: Co-culture of hair follicles with ILC1lc triggered immune privilege collapse, as evidenced by ectopic and overexpressed HLA-A,B,C, ß2-microglobulin, and HLA-DR.
source: Indeed, the co-culture of HFs with ILC1lc triggered IP collapse, as evidenced by ectopic and overexpressed HLA-A,B,C, ß2-microglobulin (ß2 MG), and HLA-DR, along with overexpression of the 'danger'/tissue distress signals, MICA and CD1d, which interact with and stimulate NKG2D (Uchida et al., 2021; Fan et al., 2022) as compared to HFs interacting with PBMC/PHA or with ILC3 cells (Figure 5A, B, C, D, E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 5A-F.

claim: Co-culture of hair follicles with ILC1lc resulted in overexpression of MICA and CD1d.
source: Indeed, the co-culture of HFs with ILC1lc triggered IP collapse, as evidenced by ectopic and overexpressed HLA-A,B,C, ß2-microglobulin (ß2 MG), and HLA-DR, along with overexpression of the 'danger'/tissue distress signals, MICA and CD1d, which interact with and stimulate NKG2D (Uchida et al., 2021; Fan et al., 2022) as compared to HFs interacting with PBMC/PHA or with ILC3 cells (Figure 5A, B, C, D, E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 5A-F.

claim: Protein expression of TGF-β1 and α-MSH almost disappeared in the epithelium of hair follicles co-cultured with autologous ILC1lc or CD8+/NKG2D+ cells.
source: Notably, quantitative immunohistomorphoemtry (qIHM) also showed that protein expression of the immunoinhibitory HF-IP guardians, TGF-β1 and α-MSH (Gilhar et al., 2012; Bertolini et al., 2020; Paus et al., 2018; Ito et al., 2004), almost disappeared in the epithelium of HFs co-cultured with autologous ILC1lc or CD8+/NKG2D+ cells (=positive control) (Figure 5G, H and I)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunohistomorphometry data presented in Figure 5G-I.

claim: Adding anti-NKG2D blocking antibodies prevented hair follicle immune privilege collapse and preserved the immune privilege in the ILC1lc /NKG2D treated group.
source: Importantly, adding anti-NKG2D blocking antibodies prevented HFs IP collapse and preserved the IP in the ILC1lc /NKG2D treated group (Figure 5G, H and I).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 5G-I.

claim: ILC1lc significantly accelerated the transformation of anagen into catagen hair follicles ex vivo compared to ILC2, ILC3, or PBMCs/PHA.
source: This showed that ILC1lc significantly accelerated the transformation of anagen into catagen HFs ex vivo (Paus et al., 2005) compared to all three negative controls (ILC2, ILC3, or PBMCs/PHA) – thus eliciting the third hallmark of the AA phenotype besides HF-IP collapse and dystrophy ex vivo (Gilhar et al., 2012; Bertolini et al., 2020; Messenger et al., 1986; Figure 6A)
evidence: The claim is supported by hair cycle analysis data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: ILC1lc produced and secreted higher amounts of IFN-γ into the medium than all other cells co-cultured with 'stressed' hair follicles, including CD8+/NKG2D+ cells.
source: ELISA analysis revealed that ILC1lc produced and secreted higher amounts of IFN-γ into the medium than all other cells co-cultured with 'stressed' HFs, including CD8+/NKG2D+ cells (p<0.05) (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: ILC1lc showed significantly increased intracellular IFN-γ expression when co-cultured with 'stressed,' autologous hair follicles.
source: FACS analysis showed ILC1lc activation when these were co-cultured with 'stressed,' autologous HFs (600 cells/HF), as evidenced by significantly increased intracellular IFN-γ expression by ILC1lc (Bernink et al., 2017) (93 ± 11%) compared to the positive control (CD8+/NKG2D+, 75 ± 9%, p<0.05) (Figure 6C)
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: Neutralizing anti-IFN-γ antibodies significantly reduced premature catagen development of hair follicles co-cultured with ILC1lc.
source: When neutralizing anti- IFN-γ antibodies were administered into the medium of the organ culture, premature catagen development of HFs co-cultured with ILC1lc was significantly reduced (Figure 6A), strongly suggesting that premature catagen induction by ILC1lc depends on their IFN-γsecretion (Seillet et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by hair cycle analysis data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: Reduced catagen induction was observed after adding NKG2D-blocking antibodies to the medium of hair follicles co-cultured with ILC1lc.
source: Importantly, reduced catagen induction was also seen after adding NKG2D-blocking antibodies to the medium (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by hair cycle analysis data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: ILC1lc activation and IFN-γ secretion are induced by NKG2D-stimulating danger signals overexpressed by stressed hair follicle epithelium, such as MICA.
source: This suggests that ILC1lc activation and IFN-γsecretion are induced by NKG2D-stimulating danger signals overexpressed by stressed HF epithelium, such as MICA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results showing that NKG2D blocking reduces ILC1lc effects.

claim: Significant AA-like hair loss was observed macroscopically in the xenotransplants injected with ILC1lc compared to the negative control, at about the same level as positive control xenotransplants.
source: When measured 45 days later, significant AA-like hair loss was observed macroscopically in the xenotransplants injected with ILC1lc compared to the negative control, at about the same level as positive control xenotransplants (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by macroscopic hair count data presented in Figure 7A.

claim: Anti-CD3/OKT3 antibodies failed to abrogate hair loss induction in mice treated with ILC1lc alone.
source: This showed that anti-CD3 failed to abrogate hair loss induction in the mice treated with ILC1lc alone, but suppressed hair loss in the group treated with enriched CD8/NKG2D cells, as expected (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo experimental data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Anti-CD3/OKT3 antibodies suppressed hair loss in the group treated with enriched CD8/NKG2D cells.
source: This showed that anti-CD3 failed to abrogate hair loss induction in the mice treated with ILC1lc alone, but suppressed hair loss in the group treated with enriched CD8/NKG2D cells, as expected (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo experimental data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ILC1lc induced hair follicle dystrophy, miniaturization and perifollicular lymphocytic infiltrate around anagen hair follicles in vivo.
source: Immunohistology revealed that ILC1lc, just like autologous enriched CD8/NKG2D cells, induced a phenocopy of AA immunopathology in previously healthy human scalp skin in vivo, in sharp contrast to the negative control PBMCs/PHA group: HFs dystrophy, miniaturization and perifollicular lymphocytic infiltrate around anagen HFs (Figure 7B)
evidence: The claim is supported by histology data presented in Figure 7B.

claim: ILC1lc induced immune privilege collapse in vivo, characterized by significantly increased expression of HLA-A,B,C, β2 MG, and HLA-DR of the hair follicle epithelium, along with downregulation of α-MSH and TGF-β1.
source: as well as induction of HF-IP collapse (significantly increased expression of HLA-A,B,C, β2 MG, and HLA-DR of the HF epithelium, along with downregulation of the immune privilege guardians, α-MSH and TGF-β1) (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 7C-F.

claim: IFN-γ+ cells were found to be increased around the bulb of xenotransplants injected with ILC1lc.
source: In line with the key role of IFN-γ in the development of AA (Gilhar et al., 2012; Gilhar et al., 2019a), IFN-γ+ cells were found to be increased around the bulb of xenotransplants injected with ILC1lc, even in the presence of the anti-CD3 antibody (OKT3), or with enriched CD8/NKG2D cells, but not with PHA-treated PBMCs or enriched CD8/NKG2D cells in the presence of OKT3 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B,C,D,E,F and G and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B,C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Dense infiltration of ILC1lc was found only in xenotransplants treated with the purified ILC1lc.
source: while dense infiltration of ILC1lc was found only in xenotransplants treated with the purified ILC1lc (Figure 7—figure supplement 3E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 3E-F.

claim: The peri- and intrafollicular distribution and mean number of ILC1lc in human skin xenotransplants injected with enriched CD8/NKG2D cells imitated that of ILC1lc seen in spontaneously developed hair loss lesions of AA patients.
source: Interestingly, qIHM also showed that the peri- and intrafollicular distribution and mean number of ILC1lc in human skin xenotransplants injected with enriched CD8/NKG2D cells imitated that of ILC1lc seen in spontaneously developed hair loss lesions of AA patients, further supporting the role of ILC1lc in human AA (Figure 1A, B, C and D, Figure 8A, B, C and D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunohistomorphometry data comparing patient samples (Figure 1) and xenotransplant samples (Figure 8).

claim: CD8+/NKG2D+lymphocytes significantly outnumbered ILC1lc in the experimentally induced AA lesions.
source: Yet, CD8+/NKG2D+lymphocytes significantly outnumbered ILC1lc in the experimentally induced AA lesions (p<0.01) (Figure 8E and F), just as they do in human AA patients (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunohistomorphometry data presented in Figure 8E-F.

claim: This study is the first to phenotypically and functionally explore the role of Eomes+ILC1lc in human AA in vivo and ex vivo.
source: The current study is the first to phenotypically and functionally explore the role of Eomes +ILC1 lc in human AA in vivo and ex vivo.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study, supported by the comprehensive experimental data presented.

claim: ILC1lc provide the first functional evidence that expanded circulating autologous human ILC1lc suffice to induce all hallmarks of the AA hair loss phenotype in previously healthy, organ-cultured human scalp hair follicles ex vivo.
source: Here, we show that ILC1lc are increased in AA lesions provide the first functional evidence that expanded circulating autologous human ILC1lc suffice to induce all hallmarks of the AA hair loss phenotype (premature catagen, HF dystrophy, and HF-IP collapse) in previously healthy, organ-cultured human scalp HFs ex vivo
evidence: The claim is supported by the comprehensive ex vivo experimental data presented in Figures 3-6.

claim: ILC1lc suffice to induce all hallmarks of the AA hair loss phenotype in human scalp skin xenotransplants in vivo.
source: Here, we show that ILC1lc are increased in AA lesions provide the first functional evidence that expanded circulating autologous human ILC1lc suffice to induce all hallmarks of the AA hair loss phenotype (premature catagen, HF dystrophy, and HF-IP collapse) in previously healthy, organ-cultured human scalp HFs ex vivo and in human scalp skin xenotransplants in vivo, where they also cause the characteristic clinical hair loss phenomenon.
evidence: The claim is supported by the in vivo experimental data presented in Figures 7-8.

claim: This study provides the first unequivocal functional evidence of a key role of ILC1lc innate lymphocytes in a model human autoimmune disease.
source: This also provides the first unequivocal functional evidence of a key role of ILC1lc innate lymphocytes in a model human autoimmune disease, and thus identifies these lymphocytes as important novel targets in future AA therapy.
evidence: The claim is supported by the comprehensive experimental data showing ILC1lc can induce AA.

claim: IFN-γ secretion and NKG2D signaling are both required for ILC1lc to induce AA-pattern hair follicle damage.
source: Mechanistically, we demonstrate that IFN-γsecretion and NKG2D signaling are both required for this AA-pattern HF damage to occur (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that blocking IFN-γ or NKG2D reduces ILC1lc effects (Figures 5-6).

claim: ILC1lc interact directly with human hair follicles rather than affecting them only indirectly.
source: That ILC1lc alone can induce all hallmarks of AA in a healthy human (mini-) organ ex vivo and in vivo, presumably in an autoantigen-independent manner, also demonstrates that these innate/transitional lymphocytes interact directly with human HFs, rather than affecting them only indirectly.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results showing ILC1lc alone can induce AA.

claim: Resident T-cells in human scalp skin transplants are not responsible for the AA-inducing effects of ILC1lc in vivo.
source: We also show that resident T-cells in human scalp skin transplants are not responsible for the AA-inducing effects of ILC1lc in vivo (Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing anti-CD3 antibodies do not prevent ILC1lc-induced AA (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: CD8+ T cells are not the only drivers of AA disease.
source: Our study demonstrates that CD8+ T cells, which have long been thought to represent the central players in AA pathobiology (Pratt et al., 2017; Xing et al., 2014; de Jong et al., 2018; Gilhar et al., 1998; Wang et al., 2016; Paus et al., 1993), are not the only drivers of disease (Gilhar et al., 2019a; Pratt et al., 2017; de Jong et al., 2018; Paus et al., 1993)
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data showing ILC1lc alone can induce AA, and by citations to published literature.

claim: The characteristic hair loss pattern diagnosed as AA phenotype does not always represent a classical, autoantigen- and autoreactive CD8+/NKGD2+T-cell-dependent autoimmune disease.
source: The study further supports the concept that the characteristic hair loss pattern we diagnose as AA phenotype, does not always represent a classical, autoantigen- and autoreactive CD8+/NKGD2 +T-cell-dependent autoimmune disease ('autoimmune AA' [AAA]), but can also reflect non-autoimmune pathomechanisms that may perhaps best be defined as non-autoimmune AA subtype (NAIAA) (Bertolini et al., 2020; Paus et al., 2018; Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data and citations to published literature proposing the AAA/NAIAA distinction.

claim: An AA-subtype that began as NAIAA can over time transform into the AAA-variant in a state of prolonged hair follicle immune privilege collapse.
source: In a state of prolonged HF-IP collapse and thus chronic exposure of HF-associated autoantigens to (pre-existent?) autoreactive CD8 +T cells, it is well conceivable that an AA-subtype that began as NAIAA can over time transform into the AAA-variant, thus explaining the chronic-intermittent course that is seen in so many autoimmune diseases.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental findings and known features of autoimmune diseases.

claim: The novel concept of ILC1-induced NAIAA mandates a differential, personalized management approach to future AA therapy.
source: The novel concept of ILC1-induced NAIAA mandates a differential, personalized management approach to future AA therapy, which tailors treatment to the specific pathobiology at hand in any given AA patient.
evidence: This is an inference and recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: Future AA therapy must include the targeting of pathogenic, potently IFN-γ-secreting ILC1lc, at least when these are seen to be increased in lesional AA biopsies.
source: This must now include the targeting of pathogenic, potently IFN-γ -secreting ILC1lc, at least when these are seen to be increased in lesional AA biopsies.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: ILC1lc are even more potent IFN-γ producers than CD8+T cells.
source: In fact, we demonstrate here that ILC1lc are even more potent IFN-γproducers than CD8 +T cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA and FACS data presented in Figure 6B-C.

claim: The selective tissue distribution of ILC1lc makes them ideally localized to provide an early source of cytokines to initiate/trigger pro-inflammatory immune responses directed against distressed tissues.
source: Also, despite the relatively low numbers of ILC1lc, their selective tissue distribution makes them ideally localized to provide an early source of cytokines to initiate/trigger pro-inflammatory immune responses directed against distressed tissues (Vivier, 2021), as documented here in our co-culture assay with 'stressed' human scalp HFs ex vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature and the experimental data from the co-culture assay.

claim: IL-12 and IL-18 may be involved in the early stages of AA development by stimulating IFN-γ production from resident IL-12Rß2+immune cells.
source: That IL-12 and IL-18 were among the cytokines used here to facilitate ILC1lc isolation from human PBMCs is also interesting in the context of our most recent observation that local IL-12 signaling, supported by IL-18, may be involved in the early stages of AA development by stimulating IFN-γ production from resident IL-12Rß2+immune cells, eventually leading to HF-IP collapse (Edelkamp, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Treatment with IL-12 +IL-18 of healthy hair follicles selectively enriches IFN-γ-inducible genes and promotes the release of IFN-γ into the medium and thus hair follicle immune privilege collapse.
source: In fact, treatment with IL-12 +IL-18 of healthy HFs selectively enriches IFN-γ -inducible genes and promotes the release of IFN-γ into the medium and thus HF-IP collapse.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: IL-12 is a key effector cytokine in promoting pathogenic IFN-γ secretion and hair follicle immune privilege collapse.
source: These preliminary findings suggest that IL-12 is a key effector cytokine in promoting pathogenic IFN-γ secretion and HF-IP collapse.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited literature and the experimental context.

claim: An immunopathology-initiating role of ILC1lc has been proposed in vitiligo, inflammatory bowel disease, lupus erythematosus, and the aggravation of atherosclerosis.
source: An immunopathology-initiating role of ILC1lc is not unique to AA and has also been proposed in other inflammatory conditions (Kim et al., 2021), including vitiligo (Tulic et al., 2019), which shares some pathogenesis features with AA (Harris, 2013; Tomaszewska et al., 2020), inflammatory bowel disease (McDonald et al., 2018; Bernink et al., 2013; Tang et al., 2019), lupus erythematosus (Guo et al., 2019), and the aggravation of atherosclerosis (Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: This study is the first to demonstrate that ILC1lc can induce the full disease-mimicking immunopathology phenotype in a previously healthy human (mini-) organ.
source: Yet, to the best of our knowledge, the current study is the first to demonstrate that these innate immunocytes can indeed induce the full disease-mimicking immunopathology phenotype in a previously healthy human (mini-) organ.
evidence: The claim is supported by the comprehensive experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Abnormalities in the crosstalk between ILC1lc and gut microbiota have been observed in various diseases.
source: Also, abnormalities in the crosstalk between ILC1lc and gut microbiota have been observed in various diseases (Jiao et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Microbial dysbiosis has been reported in the scalp skin of AA patients.
source: Therefore, it is interesting to ask whether the microbial dysbiosis that has been reported in the scalp skin of AA patients (Pinto et al., 2020) may activate the very few, strategically positioned perifollicular ILC1lc present in healthy human scalp skin through abnormal crosstalk with HF microbiota (Lousada et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The study introduces IFN-γ-secreting ILC1lc lymphocytes as important novel players in human AA pathobiology and identifies them as new therapeutic intervention targets.
source: Collectively, our study introduces IFN-γ -secreting ILC1lc lymphocytes as important novel players in human AA pathobiology and identifies them as new therapeutic intervention targets.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The strategic location, capability to recognize and respond to hair follicle distress signals, excessive production of IFN-γ by ILC1lc, and their direct pathogenic effects on human hair follicles ex vivo support that these cells play a hitherto unappreciated role in early AA pathogenesis.
source: Their strategic location, their capability to recognize and respond to HF distress signals such as MICA and selected chemokines, the excessive production of IFN-γ by ILC1lc, and their direct, pathogenic effects on human HFs ex vivo documented here, all support that these cells play a hitherto unappreciated role in early AA pathogenesis.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Autoreactive CD8+T cells are not indispensable for AA induction.
source: Moreover, our study demonstrates that autoreactive CD8 +T cells are not indispensable for AA induction and further supports that non-autoimmune AA variants (NAIAA) (Bertolini et al., 2020) exist and that innate/transitional immune cells play an important role in AA pathobiology.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data showing ILC1lc alone can induce AA.

claim: Non-autoimmune AA variants (NAIAA) exist.
source: Moreover, our study demonstrates that autoreactive CD8 +T cells are not indispensable for AA induction and further supports that non-autoimmune AA variants (NAIAA) (Bertolini et al., 2020) exist and that innate/transitional immune cells play an important role in AA pathobiology.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data and a citation to published literature.

claim: Innate/transitional immune cells play an important role in AA pathobiology.
source: Moreover, our study demonstrates that autoreactive CD8 +T cells are not indispensable for AA induction and further supports that non-autoimmune AA variants (NAIAA) (Bertolini et al., 2020) exist and that innate/transitional immune cells play an important role in AA pathobiology.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.
